Empirical Research Plan – Police Presence and Property Crime in Buenos Aires after the 1994 AMIA Attack
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  

Method: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with neighborhood and day fixed effects, augmented with an instrumental-variables (2SLS) version to purge any remaining simultaneity between police and crime.  

Why it fits:  
• The AMIA bombing constituted an unexpected security shock that led to an abrupt, centralized re-allocation of officers toward neighborhoods hosting potential Jewish or other “sensitive” targets.  
• Assignment was driven by perceived terror risk, not by pre-existing property-crime trends, providing quasi-random differential shocks in police intensity.  
• We observe multiple months pre- and post-shock at a daily frequency—ideal for a DiD/event-study design.  
• Using an IV (Treated × Post) for actual police counts allows us to estimate the causal elasticity of crime with respect to police while still exploiting the DiD timing.

Baseline estimating equation (reduced form / ITT):  
Y_it = α_i + λ_t + β Treat_i × Post_t + γX_it + ε_it  

Second stage (elasticity):  
Police_it = π Treat_i × Post_t + θ_i + κ_t + υ_it  
Y_it = α_i + λ_t + ρ ŜPolice_it + γX_it + η_it  

where i = neighborhood, t = day.

2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable  
• “Police shock” = interaction Treat_i × Post_t.  
 – Treat_i = 1 if neighborhood contained (pre-attack) at least one synagogue, Jewish school, Israeli‐owned firm, embassy, or was designated a “potential target” by the federal security directive.  
 – Post_t = 1 for dates ≥ 18-July-1994 (attack date) plus any short implementation lag (e.g., 2 days).  

Control group  
• Neighborhoods with no designated targets and therefore no mandated police surge.  
• To avoid contamination we drop buffer zones within, say, 300 m of treated tracts for the core analysis.

Treatment timing / variation  
• Sharp discontinuity on the attack date.  
• Intensity varies cross-sectionally with the number/size of targets; we exploit both the binary exposure and a continuous shift-share measure (#targets_i × Post_t) in robustness checks.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Parallel trends: Absent the attack, treated and control neighborhoods would have followed similar property-crime trajectories.  
 Plausibility: Security planning unrelated to property-crime; pre-trend graphs and placebo DiD on earlier months can test.  

A2. No simultaneous shocks differentially hitting treated areas (excludability).  
 Plausibility: Other anti-crime programs were city-wide; the unique focus was anti-terror. Check city council records/media.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): Crime displaced from treated to control neighborhoods does not mechanically bias estimates.  
 Plausibility: Short-run spatial displacement is a concern. We address this by (i) measuring crime for larger catchment radii in robustness, (ii) presenting city-level totals.

A4. First-stage relevance (for IV): Treat × Post strongly predicts extra officers.  
 Plausibility: Mandated deployments were codified; we will show F-stat ≫ 10.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

T1. Displacement of officers away from control areas (negative shock).  
 Fix: Consider “pure control” neighborhoods whose officer counts changed little; include neighborhood-specific linear time trends to soak up gradual manpower drifts.

T2. Crime displacement across space.  
 Fix: Report results at multiple spatial aggregations and on city-wide total crime (difference-in-totals). If displacement is pure spatial re-sorting, total crime effect should be zero.

T3. Measurement error in daily officer counts.  
 Fix: Use agency rosters plus GPS patrol logs where available; aggregate to weekly counts in robustness; IV approach further attenuates classical error.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # high performance FE & IV
library(lubridate)    # date handling

# 1. Load data (assumes three csv files)
crime   <- fread("crime_daily_neigh.csv")      # neigh_id, date, property_crime
police  <- fread("police_daily_neigh.csv")     # neigh_id, date, officers
targets <- fread("targets_by_neigh.csv")       # neigh_id, n_targets

# 2. Merge
dt <- merge(crime, police, by = c("neigh_id","date"))
dt <- merge(dt, targets, by = "neigh_id")

# 3. Variable construction
dt[, date := ymd(date)]
attack_date <- ymd("1994-07-18")

dt[, post  := as.integer(date >= attack_date)]
dt[, treat := as.integer(n_targets > 0)]     # binary exposure
dt[, tx_post := treat * post]

# Log crime plus 1 to stay defined
dt[, ln_propcrime := log(property_crime + 1)]

# 4. Main ITT DiD (neigh & day FE)
did_itt <- feols(ln_propcrime ~ tx_post | neigh_id + date, data = dt, cluster = "neigh_id")
summary(did_itt)

# 5. 2SLS elasticities (instrument officer counts with tx_post)
iv_mod <- feols(ln_propcrime ~ 1 | neigh_id + date | officers ~ tx_post, 
                data = dt, cluster = "neigh_id")
summary(iv_mod)

# 6. Event-study visualization
dt[, rel_day := as.integer(date - attack_date)]
es <- feols(ln_propcrime ~ sunab(rel_day, treat) | neigh_id + date, 
            data = dt[abs(rel_day) <= 90], cluster = "neigh_id")
iplot(es)

# 7. Robustness: Poisson FE on raw counts
pois <- feglm(property_crime ~ tx_post | neigh_id + date, 
              data = dt, family = "poisson", cluster = "neigh_id")
summary(pois)
```

6. Expected Results  

Theory (deterrence) predicts β < 0: more police reduces property crime. Prior empirical elasticities for U.S. cities range −0.3 to −0.7. Given the sudden, visible surge, I expect a somewhat larger immediate effect: a 10 % rise in officers lowers property crime by roughly 5–8 %. That translates to ρ ≈ −0.5 to −0.8 in the 2SLS log-log specification.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = good, 0 = weak)  

1. Strong, plausibly exogenous shock (treatment exogeneity): 1  
2. Parallel pre-trends verified graphically / statistically: 0.8  
3. No interference / spillovers: 0.5  
4. Accurate measurement of key variables: 0.9  
5. Large first stage (for IV): 1  

Overall internal validity score ≈ 4.2 / 5.

This plan provides a transparent and testable framework to estimate the causal impact of increased police presence on property crime in Buenos Aires using the 1994 AMIA attack as an exogenous allocation shock.
